tool.name: Amazon DynamoDB
tool.tagline: AWS's serverless key-value and document database with single-digit-ms latency
tool.description: Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL database on AWS that stores items by key and scales to virtually any traffic with predictable low latency and no servers to run. It powers shopping carts, sessions, game state, IoT and many serverless backends. Learning it means learning to design data around access patterns instead of joins.

glossary.def: In DynamoDB, one named value inside an item, like "total": 35. An item is a set of attributes, and apart from the key each item in a table can have different ones.

In DynamoDB, one of the storage slices a table is split into. The partition key, the first part of an item's key, decides which slice holds the item; items with the same partition key are stored together.
A DynamoDB primary key made of a partition key plus a sort key. A simple key is the partition key alone.
All the items in a DynamoDB table that share one partition key, stored together and ordered by their sort key, like one customer's folder of receipts filed by date.
Python's exact decimal-number type, from the decimal module. boto3 uses it for DynamoDB numbers, because a float can't hold values like 0.1 exactly.
boto3's friendly DynamoDB table object, boto3.resource('dynamodb').Table(name): you pass and get plain Python values, and it converts them to DynamoDB's types for you.
boto3's direct interface to DynamoDB, boto3.client('dynamodb'): one method per API operation, with every value wrapped in its type code, like {"N": "35"}.
DynamoDB's own data format, where every value is wrapped with a short type code: {"total": {"N": "35"}} means total is the number 35.
A version of DynamoDB that runs on your own computer (a Java program or a Docker image), for free, safe development and testing.
A DynamoDB table setting that makes delete requests fail until someone switches it off, so a table can't be removed by accident.
A DynamoDB billing mode where you pay for each read and write and the table absorbs traffic spikes by itself, with no capacity to plan.
A DynamoDB billing mode where you reserve a fixed number of read and write units per second, often adjusted by auto scaling; cheaper for steady traffic.
DynamoDB's measure of work: one write unit is one write of up to 1 KB, one read unit is one strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB (an eventually consistent read costs half).
In DynamoDB, a short string in its own mini-language that says what an operation should change, check or return, such as SET total = :t or attribute_exists(pk).
A DynamoDB expression saying how to change an item, with up to four parts: SET, REMOVE, ADD and DELETE.
A DynamoDB expression the item must pass for a write to happen, such as attribute_not_exists(pk) or stock >= :n.
A DynamoDB expression listing which attributes a read should return, so the reply is smaller (the read still costs the same).
A DynamoDB expression that drops items from a query or scan result after they've been read; you still pay for reading them.
In a DynamoDB expression, a stand-in name: :name for a value, #name for an attribute name. The real values come from separate dictionaries passed with the call.
A DynamoDB write that only happens if a condition holds, such as 'no item with this key exists yet'. The check and the write happen as one step.
An extra way into a DynamoDB table: the same items arranged under a different key, kept up to date automatically, so you can query them by something other than the primary key.
The choice of which attributes a DynamoDB secondary index copies from the table: only the keys, a list you give, or everything.
A DynamoDB secondary index that only contains items having its key attribute, so it lists just a chosen subset, such as open orders.
Giving a DynamoDB index generic key names (GSI1PK, GSI1SK) so different kinds of items can store different values there, letting one index answer many questions.
A DynamoDB secondary index whose partition key is the table's sort key and the other way round, so a many-to-many link can be read from either side.
Spreading one very busy DynamoDB key over several keys by adding a suffix (DATE#2025-03-01#0 to #7); reads then query every suffix and combine the results.
A DynamoDB modelling style that stores several kinds of items (customers, orders) in one table with generic key names, so related items can be fetched in one query.
One specific question an app asks of its data, with its inputs, such as 'list a customer's orders, newest first'. DynamoDB tables are designed from the list of these.
To store copies of the same data in several places so it can be read in one go; normalizing is the opposite, keeping each fact in exactly one place.
The part of a DynamoDB batch request that wasn't done, returned in the reply. The caller must send those items again.
boto3's table.batch_writer(): it collects your puts and deletes, sends them in groups of 25 and resends any the table didn't process.
Splitting a DynamoDB scan into numbered segments that several workers read at the same time, to finish a whole-table read sooner.
A value a paged API hands back with each page; the caller sends it back unchanged to get the next page, without needing to understand what's inside.
An AWS service for streams of records that many programs can read, kept for up to a year; DynamoDB can send its changes there.
DynamoDB's automatic lending of a table's unused throughput to its busiest partitions, up to each partition's limit.
DynamoDB automatically splitting a partition that stays busy into more partitions, so its traffic is spread out.
A CloudWatch feature that shows which DynamoDB keys are accessed or throttled the most.
A DynamoDB table with copies (replicas) in several AWS Regions that are kept in sync; every copy accepts reads and writes.
Multi-Region eventual consistency: the default for DynamoDB global tables. A write is confirmed in its own Region and copied to the others shortly after.
Multi-Region strong consistency: a DynamoDB global table mode where writes are copied to other Regions before they're confirmed, so every Region reads the latest value.
A conflict rule for copies of data: when two places change the same thing at once, the change with the later timestamp is kept and the other is dropped.
DynamoDB Accelerator: a cache cluster that sits in front of DynamoDB with the same API, keeping recently read items in memory for very fast repeated reads.
A DynamoDB storage tier for a table: Standard, or Standard-IA (infrequent access) with cheaper storage but pricier reads and writes.
Splitting one large record into several smaller items under the same partition key, so frequent updates touch only a small item.
A cache that writes go through on their way to the database, so it holds the new value as soon as it's saved.

concepts.name: What DynamoDB is
concepts.summary: A fully managed database on AWS: tables of items you look up by key, with no servers to run and almost unlimited scale.
concepts.why: Knowing its strengths and limits up front tells you when DynamoDB is the right choice and how differently you must think about data.
concepts.body:
Most apps need somewhere to keep their data (user profiles, shopping carts, game scores) and get it back quickly. **DynamoDB** is AWS's serverless database for that. You create a **table**, write **items** into it (an item is one record, such as one user's profile), and read them back by their key in a few milliseconds, whether the table holds a megabyte or a hundred terabytes.

It's a **key-value database**: like a huge Python dictionary, every item is stored under a key and fetched by that key. Databases that don't use SQL tables the way RDS does are called **NoSQL** databases, and DynamoDB is one.

There are no instances to size, patch or fail over. AWS keeps copies of every table in three Availability Zones and grows it for you.

Each item is a set of **attributes**: named values, like the keys and values of a dictionary (`"name": "Ann"`, `"total": 35`). Apart from the key, items in one table can have completely different attributes. There's no **schema**, no fixed list of attributes every record must have. An item can be up to 400 KB (kilobytes), roughly a hundred pages of a book.

The trade-off is in asking questions of the data. There's no SQL across the whole table, no joins (combining two tables in one question) and no totals or averages worked out for you. Fast reads always go through a key: fetch one item by its **primary key**, the attribute or attributes that identify it, or fetch a group of related items that share part of their key, as the next lesson shows. Reading the whole table works, but it's slow and expensive.

So DynamoDB fits apps whose questions are known in advance, especially at high or spiky traffic: user profiles, shopping carts, records of who is logged in, game state, serverless APIs. It fits poorly when you need free-form questions for reports; then you'd copy the data to S3 and analyse it there, or use a relational database like RDS.

You talk to it from code through the AWS SDKs (in Python, the boto3 library, used throughout this course), from the AWS CLI, or by clicking in the AWS console.
takeaways: Tables hold items with any attributes; only the key attributes are required
Fast reads always go through a key
No joins or free-form questions: design for the questions you know in advance
Fully managed and serverless, with copies in three Availability Zones
pitfalls: Choosing DynamoDB for reports that need free-form filters and joins.

options: Free-form reports combining many tables
A shopping cart looked up by user id at very high traffic
Searching for words anywhere in product descriptions
Monthly reports totalling sales by any column
quiz.explain: Key-based lookups with known access patterns at scale are exactly what DynamoDB is built for.

concepts.name: Partition keys and sort keys
concepts.summary: The primary key is a partition key alone, or a partition key plus a sort key; it decides where items are stored and how you can fetch them.
concepts.why: Choosing the key is the most important design decision for any DynamoDB table and cannot be changed later.
concepts.body:
Every table has a **primary key**, chosen when you create the table and never changeable afterwards. It comes in two forms:

- **Simple key**: one attribute, the **partition key** (older docs call it the hash key). Each value identifies exactly one item, e.g. `user_id`.
- **Composite key**: a partition key plus a **sort key** (older name: range key). Many items can share a partition key as long as their sort keys differ, e.g. `customer_id` + `order_id`.

Why "partition"? DynamoDB spreads a table over many storage machines, and each slice of the table is a **partition**. To decide where an item goes, DynamoDB runs its partition key through a hash (a fingerprint calculation, like the one Python dictionaries use), and the result picks the partition.

All items with the same partition key are stored together, kept in order by their sort key. That group is called an **item collection**, like one customer's folder of receipts filed by date.

That layout explains what you can fetch efficiently:

- one item, if you know its full primary key
- one item collection: all items for one partition key, optionally narrowed with a sort key condition like `=`, `<`, `between` or `begins_with`, returned in sort-key order. This is called a **query**.

You can't efficiently ask for "all orders over 100 dollars" across every customer, because those items are spread over different partitions. Secondary indexes, a later topic, add other ways in.

Good partition keys have many different values that are used about equally (user ids, device ids). Sort keys are often built to sort usefully, such as dates written year first (`2025-03-01#A17`) or prefixes (`ORDER#...`), so that range conditions return useful slices.
concepts.code:
# Table "Orders": partition key customer_id, sort key order_id
#
# customer_id | order_id         | total | status
# ------------+------------------+-------+---------
# c1          | 2025-01-09#A11   | 20    | SHIPPED   <- item collection "c1",
# c1          | 2025-03-01#A17   | 35    | PENDING      stored together, sorted
# c1          | 2025-03-14#A20   | 12    | PENDING      by order_id
# c2          | 2025-02-02#B03   | 99    | SHIPPED   <- lives on another partition
#
# Efficient:  get c1 / 2025-03-01#A17
#             all orders of c1 in March 2025:
#               customer_id = "c1" AND begins_with(order_id, "2025-03")
# Not efficient without an index: all PENDING orders of every customer
takeaways: Primary key = partition key, or partition key + sort key
The partition key's hash decides where an item lives; items sharing it form a sorted item collection
A query targets one partition key and can narrow and order by the sort key
Build sort keys (dates, prefixes) so range conditions return useful slices
pitfalls: Using a partition key with only a few different values, such as status or country, which piles traffic onto a few partitions.

quiz.q: A table's key is (customer_id, order_id). Which request can DynamoDB serve efficiently?
options: All orders for customer c1 whose order_id begins with 2025-03
All orders with total > 50 across all customers
The 10 most expensive orders overall
All customers whose name starts with A
quiz.explain: It targets one partition key and uses a sort key condition, so it reads a single sorted item collection.

concepts.name: Attribute types and boto3
concepts.summary: DynamoDB's attribute types (string, number, bytes, true/false, empty, map, list, sets) and how Python's boto3 library converts them.
concepts.why: Number-type mismatches, especially floats versus Decimals, are the first errors every Python developer hits.
concepts.body:
Every attribute value has one of these types (the short codes are DynamoDB's own names):

- single values: **S** (string), **N** (number), **B** (binary: raw bytes, such as a small image), **BOOL** (true or false) and **NULL** (no value, like Python's `None`)
- documents: **M** (map: named values nested inside, like a dict) and **L** (list, any mix of types)
- sets: **SS**, **NS**, **BS** (unique strings, numbers or binaries; never empty)

Key attributes must be S, N or B. Numbers travel as text and are stored exactly, with up to 38 digits, so they're exact decimal numbers, unlike Python floats, which can't hold values like 0.1 exactly.

From Python you use **boto3**, the AWS SDK for Python (`pip install boto3`). It offers two ways in. The **low-level client** (`boto3.client("dynamodb")`) uses DynamoDB's own format, where every value is wrapped with its type code: `{"total": {"N": "35"}}`. The **Table resource** (`boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table(...)`) converts between Python values and DynamoDB types for you:

- `str` to S, `bool` to BOOL, `None` to NULL, `dict` to M, `list` to L, `set` to a set type, `bytes` to B
- numbers come back as `Decimal` (from Python's `decimal` module, an exact decimal-number type), and you must send `int` or `Decimal`, **not `float`**

Passing a float raises `TypeError: Float types are not supported`. Convert with `Decimal(str(x))`, or keep money in whole cents. When you return items as JSON from your own API, convert Decimals back first (e.g. with a `default=` function in `json.dumps`).

The Table resource is the most readable for scripts and is used in most of this course; the client offers every operation and is needed for some newer features.
concepts.code:
from decimal import Decimal
import boto3

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("Orders")

table.put_item(Item={
    "customer_id": "c1", "order_id": "2025-03-01#A17",
    "total": Decimal("35.90"),          # not 35.90 (float raises TypeError)
    "paid": True,
    "items": [{"sku": "pen", "qty": 2}],  # list of maps
    "tags": {"gift", "express"},          # string set
})
item = table.get_item(Key={"customer_id": "c1", "order_id": "2025-03-01#A17"})["Item"]
print(item["total"], type(item["total"]).__name__)   # 35.90 Decimal
print(item["items"][0]["qty"])                       # 2  (also a Decimal)
takeaways: Types: S, N, B, BOOL, NULL, M, L and the sets SS/NS/BS
Key attributes must be string, number or binary
The Table resource converts Python types automatically; numbers come back as Decimal
Never send floats: use Decimal or integers
pitfalls: Passing a Python float to put_item and getting 'Float types are not supported'.

quiz.q: Why does boto3's Table.put_item reject the value 9.99 (a float)?
options: DynamoDB cannot store fractional numbers
Only key attributes can be numbers
Numbers must be sent as strings by the caller
Floats would lose precision, so boto3 requires Decimal or int
quiz.explain: DynamoDB numbers are exact decimals, so boto3 refuses floats, which are often slightly off, and asks for Decimal.

concepts.name: Creating tables and DynamoDB Local
concepts.summary: Create a table with boto3, choose on-demand billing, wait until it is ready, and practise on DynamoDB Local.
concepts.why: You need a table to do anything, and a local copy of DynamoDB makes development fast, free and safe.
concepts.body:
`create_table` needs only the key: which attributes form the primary key, and their types. Other attributes are never declared.

- `KeySchema`: the partition key (`HASH`) and optional sort key (`RANGE`)
- `AttributeDefinitions`: name and type (`S`, `N`, `B`) for every key attribute, including keys of indexes, and nothing else
- `BillingMode`: `PAY_PER_REQUEST` (**on-demand mode**: pay for each request, nothing to plan) or `PROVISIONED`, where you reserve a fixed amount of capacity with `ProvisionedThroughput`

Creating a table takes a few seconds, and the call returns before it's done: the table starts in the `CREATING` state. So call `table.wait_until_exists()`, which checks repeatedly until the table is `ACTIVE`, before writing to it.

For development, run **DynamoDB Local**, a version of DynamoDB that runs on your own computer (a Java program, or the `amazon/dynamodb-local` Docker image). Point boto3 at it with `endpoint_url="http://localhost:8000"`. It accepts any credentials and Region, costs nothing and can't harm real data. For automated tests in Python, the `moto` library imitates DynamoDB inside the test itself.

In real projects, tables are usually created not by a Python script but from a file describing the setup, which a tool such as CloudFormation or Terraform turns into real resources; the settings are the same ones you see here. On any table that matters, turn on **point-in-time recovery** (restore the table to any second of the last 35 days) and **deletion protection** (delete requests fail until you switch it off). Each is a single setting.

Table names are unique within one account and Region.
concepts.code:
import boto3

# docker run -p 8000:8000 amazon/dynamodb-local
ddb = boto3.resource("dynamodb", endpoint_url="http://localhost:8000",
                     region_name="us-east-1",
                     aws_access_key_id="x", aws_secret_access_key="x")

table = ddb.create_table(
    TableName="Orders",
    KeySchema=[{"AttributeName": "customer_id", "KeyType": "HASH"},
               {"AttributeName": "order_id", "KeyType": "RANGE"}],
    AttributeDefinitions=[{"AttributeName": "customer_id", "AttributeType": "S"},
                          {"AttributeName": "order_id", "AttributeType": "S"}],
    BillingMode="PAY_PER_REQUEST",
)
table.wait_until_exists()
print(table.table_status)        # ACTIVE
print(table.key_schema[0])       # {'AttributeName': 'customer_id', 'KeyType': 'HASH'}
takeaways: Declare only key attributes in AttributeDefinitions
`PAY_PER_REQUEST` (on-demand) avoids capacity planning
Wait for ACTIVE before using a new table
Develop against DynamoDB Local or moto, not production
pitfalls: Listing non-key attributes in AttributeDefinitions, which makes create_table fail with a ValidationException.

quiz.q: Which attributes go into AttributeDefinitions when creating a table?
options: Every attribute your items will have
Only the partition key
Only attributes used as keys of the table or its indexes
None; DynamoDB infers them
quiz.explain: DynamoDB is schemaless except for keys, so only key attributes (table and index) are declared.

concepts.name: Put, get, update and delete items
concepts.summary: The four single-item operations, put_item, get_item, update_item and delete_item, all addressed by the item's full primary key.
concepts.why: Single-item operations by key are the bread and butter of every DynamoDB application.
concepts.body:
All single-item operations take the **full primary key** (the partition key, plus the sort key if the table has one).

- `put_item(Item=...)` writes a whole item. If an item with that key exists, it is **replaced entirely**: attributes you didn't include are gone.
- `get_item(Key=...)` reads one item. The reply contains `Item` only if the item exists, so use `resp.get("Item")`.
- `update_item(Key=..., UpdateExpression=...)` changes some attributes in place, and creates the item if it doesn't exist yet (an **upsert**: update or insert). The little `SET ...` language is covered in a later lesson. `ReturnValues="ALL_NEW"` gives back the updated item, saving a separate read.
- `delete_item(Key=...)` removes an item; deleting a missing item is not an error.

Reads are **eventually consistent** by default: DynamoDB keeps three copies of each item, and a read straight after a write may reach a copy that hasn't caught up yet (it usually does within a second). Pass `ConsistentRead=True` for a **strongly consistent** read, which always sees the latest write.

Each write to one item is **atomic**: it happens completely or not at all, and nobody ever sees it half done. All four operations also accept a `ConditionExpression` (covered later), so they only happen if the item is in an expected state.

Remember the difference: put replaces, update merges. Use `update_item` for counters, status changes and partial edits, and `put_item` when you own the whole item.

A **projection expression** (`ProjectionExpression=` on `get_item`) returns only the attributes you list. That makes the reply smaller, but not the read cheaper: you still pay for reading the full item.
concepts.code:
import boto3

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("Orders")
key = {"customer_id": "c1", "order_id": "2025-03-01#A17"}

table.put_item(Item={**key, "total": 35, "status": "PENDING"})

resp = table.update_item(
    Key=key,
    UpdateExpression="SET #s = :s",
    ExpressionAttributeNames={"#s": "status"},      # #s stands in for "status", a word DynamoDB reserves
    ExpressionAttributeValues={":s": "SHIPPED"},
    ReturnValues="ALL_NEW",
)
print(resp["Attributes"]["status"])                 # SHIPPED

print(table.get_item(Key=key)["Item"]["total"])     # 35
table.delete_item(Key=key)
print(table.get_item(Key=key).get("Item"))          # None
takeaways: Every single-item call needs the full primary key
put_item replaces the whole item; update_item changes attributes and upserts
get_item returns no Item key when the item doesn't exist
Use ReturnValues to get the new or old item back from a write
pitfalls: Using put_item to change one attribute and accidentally wiping all the others.

quiz.q: An item has attributes a, b and c. You call put_item with the same key and only attribute a. What is stored?
options: a, b and c with a updated
Only a (plus the key)
An error is raised because b and c are missing
Two items with the same key
quiz.explain: put_item replaces the whole item, so attributes not supplied are removed.

concepts.name: Query an item collection
concepts.summary: Query all items for one partition key, narrow them with a sort key condition, sort them either way and limit how many come back.
concepts.why: Query is the efficient way to read many items, and the operation most designs are built on.
concepts.body:
`Query` reads items from **one** item collection. You must give an exact match on the partition key, and you may add one condition on the sort key: `=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `between` or `begins_with`.

With the Table resource you build these conditions with `Key` from `boto3.dynamodb.conditions`:

```python
Key("customer_id").eq("c1") & Key("order_id").begins_with("2025-03")
```

Results come back **sorted by sort key**, smallest first. `ScanIndexForward=False` returns them largest first, and together with `Limit=1` that's the usual way to get the latest item (most recent order, last reading of a sensor).

Because a query reads one continuous run of items stored together, its cost depends only on how much data it reads, not on the size of the table. That's why designs that turn every question into a query scale so well.

A query returns at most 1 MB of data per call. If there's more, the reply contains `LastEvaluatedKey`, and you call again passing it as `ExclusiveStartKey` (the pagination lesson covers this).

A **filter expression** (`FilterExpression=`) can drop items after they're read, but you still pay for reading them: filters are a convenience, not a substitute for good keys.
concepts.code:
import boto3
from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("Orders")
for oid in ["2025-01-09#A11", "2025-03-01#A17", "2025-03-14#A20"]:
    table.put_item(Item={"customer_id": "c1", "order_id": oid})

march = table.query(
    KeyConditionExpression=Key("customer_id").eq("c1")
                           & Key("order_id").begins_with("2025-03"))
print([i["order_id"] for i in march["Items"]])
# ['2025-03-01#A17', '2025-03-14#A20']

latest = table.query(KeyConditionExpression=Key("customer_id").eq("c1"),
                     ScanIndexForward=False, Limit=1)
print(latest["Items"][0]["order_id"])   # 2025-03-14#A20
takeaways: Query needs an exact partition key and allows one sort key condition
Results are ordered by sort key; ScanIndexForward=False reverses them
Cost depends on the items read, not the table size
A filter expression runs after the read and doesn't reduce cost
pitfalls: Expecting a FilterExpression to make a query cheaper; you pay for everything read before filtering.

quiz.q: How do you get the most recent order for c1 when order_id starts with a date written year first?
options: Query c1 with ScanIndexForward=False and Limit=1
Scan the table and sort in Python
Query c1 with Limit=1 (ascending)
get_item with only the partition key
quiz.explain: Descending order by sort key plus a limit of one returns the item with the largest order_id.

concepts.name: Scan and pagination
concepts.summary: Read a whole table with Scan, page through any result with LastEvaluatedKey, and use parallel scans for big jobs.
concepts.why: Every listing needs pagination, and knowing why Scan is expensive keeps it out of code that users wait on.
concepts.body:
`Scan` reads **every item** in a table or index, optionally dropping some with a filter expression. You pay for everything it reads, so on a large table it's slow and costly. Use it for exports, migrations and admin jobs, not while a user waits.

Both Query and Scan return at most **1 MB** per call (or `Limit` items read). When more data remains, the reply includes `LastEvaluatedKey`; pass it as `ExclusiveStartKey` in the next call, and keep going until the key is absent. Note that `Limit` caps the items **read**, before filtering, so a page can come back with fewer items than `Limit`, or even none, while more pages remain.

If your own API returns pages to its callers, hand them `LastEvaluatedKey` as a **pagination cursor**: a value they send back to get the next page, without needing to understand it. It's a dict, so you typically turn it into JSON text and then into base64 (plain letters and digits, safe to put in a URL). DynamoDB has no page numbers: you can't jump to page 7.

For big jobs, a **parallel scan** splits the table into `TotalSegments` pieces and lets several workers (separate programs running at once) each scan one `Segment` at the same time. For full exports to analytics, the managed **Export to S3** feature is better still: it works from a backup and uses none of the table's capacity.

The low-level client also offers **paginators** (`client.get_paginator("query")`), helpers that run this loop for you.
concepts.code:
import boto3

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("Orders")

def scan_all(table, **kwargs):
    """Yield every item, following LastEvaluatedKey page by page."""
    while True:
        page = table.scan(**kwargs)
        yield from page["Items"]
        if "LastEvaluatedKey" not in page:
            return
        kwargs["ExclusiveStartKey"] = page["LastEvaluatedKey"]

with table.batch_writer() as bw:                 # writes many items efficiently (see batch lesson)
    for n in range(250):
        bw.put_item(Item={"customer_id": f"c{n % 7}", "order_id": f"o{n:04}"})

print(sum(1 for _ in scan_all(table, Limit=40)))   # 250  (7 pages of up to 40)
takeaways: Scan reads and bills for every item, filter or not
Pages are at most 1 MB; follow LastEvaluatedKey until it's missing
Limit counts items read before filtering
Prefer Export to S3 or parallel scans for whole-table jobs
pitfalls: Treating an empty page as the end of results while LastEvaluatedKey is still present.

quiz.q: A Scan with Limit=100 and a FilterExpression returns 0 items and a LastEvaluatedKey. What does that mean?
options: The table is empty
The scan failed and must be retried
The filter is invalid
100 items were evaluated, none matched, and more items remain
quiz.explain: Limit applies before filtering; the presence of LastEvaluatedKey means there are more pages to read.

concepts.name: Update, condition and projection expressions
concepts.summary: Write update expressions with SET, REMOVE, ADD and DELETE, plus placeholders for names and values.
concepts.why: Expressions are how you change, protect and trim items, and their syntax trips everyone up at first.
concepts.body:
DynamoDB doesn't use SQL. Instead, several operations take short **expressions**: little strings in DynamoDB's own mini-language, such as `SET total = :t`, that say what to change, check or return.

An **update expression** has up to four parts, each used once:

- `SET a = :v, b = b + :one, c = if_not_exists(c, :zero), l = list_append(l, :new)` sets values, does arithmetic, fills in defaults and appends to lists
- `REMOVE attr, list[0]` deletes attributes or list elements
- `ADD counter :n` adds to a number (starting from 0 if it's missing) or adds elements to a set
- `DELETE tags :old` removes elements from a set

Nested values are reached with dots and positions: `address.city`, `items[2].qty`.

Values are never written straight into the expression. Use **placeholders**: `:name` stands for a value supplied in `ExpressionAttributeValues`, and `#name` stands for an attribute name supplied in `ExpressionAttributeNames`. You need `#name` for names DynamoDB keeps for its own use (`status`, `name`, `date`, `count` and hundreds more) or that contain special characters.

A **condition expression** is a test the item must pass: comparisons, `AND/OR/NOT`, `BETWEEN`, `IN`, and functions like `attribute_exists(a)`, `attribute_not_exists(a)`, `begins_with`, `contains` and `size`. A projection expression lists the attributes to return. With the Table resource you can write conditions as `Attr("x").gt(1)` objects instead of strings.

`ADD` and `SET x = x + :n` are atomic increments: two programs can add at the same moment without reading first, and neither addition is lost.
concepts.code:
import boto3

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("Orders")
key = {"customer_id": "c9", "order_id": "o1"}
table.put_item(Item={**key, "tags": {"new"}, "notes": "fragile"})

r = table.update_item(
    Key=key,
    UpdateExpression=("SET #st = :st, page_views = if_not_exists(page_views, :zero) + :one "
                      "REMOVE notes ADD tags :t"),
    ExpressionAttributeNames={"#st": "status"},
    ExpressionAttributeValues={":st": "PAID", ":zero": 0, ":one": 1, ":t": {"vip"}},
    ReturnValues="ALL_NEW",
)
item = r["Attributes"]
print(item["status"], item["page_views"], sorted(item["tags"]), "notes" in item)
# PAID 1 ['new', 'vip'] False
takeaways: Update expression parts: SET, REMOVE, ADD, DELETE
Values go in `:placeholders`, reserved or odd names in `#placeholders`
`if_not_exists` and `ADD` give safe defaults and atomic counters
Conditions use functions like attribute_exists and begins_with
pitfalls: Writing an attribute called status or name directly in an expression and getting an error because DynamoDB reserves that word.

quiz.q: Two clients call update_item with 'ADD views :one' on the same item at the same moment. What is the final increase?
options: 1, because one update overwrites the other
It depends on which client reads first
2, because ADD is applied atomically on the server
An error, because concurrent updates conflict
quiz.explain: The increment happens inside DynamoDB per request, so both are applied without a read-modify-write race.

concepts.name: Conditional writes and optimistic locking
concepts.summary: Make writes succeed only if the item is in an expected state: create-only puts, guarded updates and version numbers.
concepts.why: Conditions are DynamoDB's way to stay correct when several programs write at once, without locking items first.
concepts.body:
Any put, update or delete can carry a `ConditionExpression`. DynamoDB checks it against the current item **atomically** with the write: if it's false, nothing is written and the call fails with `ConditionalCheckFailedException`. A write like this is called a **conditional write**.

Common patterns:

- **Create only if new**: `put_item(..., ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(customer_id)")`. Checking that the partition key attribute is missing is the usual way to say "no item with this key exists".
- **Guard a change of state**: `update_item(... SET #s = :shipped, ConditionExpression="#s = :paid")`, so an order can only ship once it's paid.
- **Never go below zero**: `SET stock = stock - :n` with the condition `stock >= :n`.
- **Optimistic locking**: keep a `version` number in the item. Read the item, change it, then write with `version = :read_version` as the condition and `version = version + 1` in the update. If someone else wrote in between, the version no longer matches, your write fails, and you re-read and try again. It's "optimistic" because you expect conflicts to be rare and only check at the end.

Catch the error via `client.exceptions.ConditionalCheckFailedException` (from the Table resource: `table.meta.client.exceptions...`). Add `ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure="ALL_OLD"` to get the current item back inside the error and save another read.

A failed condition still uses, and bills, write capacity.
concepts.code:
import boto3

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("Orders")
errors = table.meta.client.exceptions
key = {"customer_id": "c5", "order_id": "o1"}

table.put_item(Item={**key, "stock": 3, "version": 1},
               ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(customer_id)")
try:  # same key again: refused
    table.put_item(Item={**key, "stock": 0, "version": 1},
                   ConditionExpression="attribute_not_exists(customer_id)")
except errors.ConditionalCheckFailedException:
    print("already exists")                    # already exists

def take(n, seen_version):
    table.update_item(Key=key,
        UpdateExpression="SET stock = stock - :n, version = version + :one",
        ConditionExpression="stock >= :n AND version = :v",
        ExpressionAttributeValues={":n": n, ":one": 1, ":v": seen_version})

take(2, 1)                                     # ok: stock 1, version 2
try:
    take(1, 1)                                 # stale version
except errors.ConditionalCheckFailedException:
    print("conflict, re-read and retry")       # conflict, re-read and retry
takeaways: Conditions are checked atomically with the write
`attribute_not_exists(pk)` means create-only
Version attributes implement optimistic locking
Handle ConditionalCheckFailedException as an expected outcome
pitfalls: Reading an item, checking a value in application code and then writing without a condition: another writer can slip in between.

quiz.q: What happens when a conditional update's condition is false?
options: The update is applied and a warning returned
Nothing is written and ConditionalCheckFailedException is raised
DynamoDB waits until the condition becomes true
The item is deleted
quiz.explain: A false condition aborts the write and raises an exception the caller handles.

concepts.name: Global and local secondary indexes
concepts.summary: Add global and local secondary indexes to query by other attributes, choose what they copy, and know their consistency and limits.
concepts.why: Most real tables need more than one access pattern, and indexes are how DynamoDB serves them.
concepts.body:
So far you could only fetch items by their primary key. A **secondary index** gives the same items a second key, kept up to date automatically, that you `Query` (or `Scan`) by passing `IndexName=...`. Like the index at the back of a book, it's another way to find the same pages.

A **global secondary index (GSI)** has its own partition key and optional sort key, made from any attributes you like. It's effectively a separate copy of the table that DynamoDB updates **asynchronously**, a moment after each write:

- reads from it are only eventually consistent
- it has its own capacity: on a table where you reserve capacity in advance, giving a GSI too little slows down (throttles) writes to the main table
- you can add or delete it at any time; the default limit is 20 per table
- keys don't have to be unique in an index

A **local secondary index (LSI)** keeps the table's partition key but uses a different sort key. It must be created together with the table, supports strongly consistent reads, and limits each item collection to 10 GB. Up to 5 per table. Prefer GSIs unless you need strongly consistent reads in the other sort order.

**Projections** decide which attributes are copied into the index: `KEYS_ONLY`, `INCLUDE` (a list you give) or `ALL`. A query on an index returns only projected attributes; copying more costs more storage and write capacity.

Only items that have the index key attributes appear in the index. That's useful: it enables sparse indexes, covered later.
concepts.code:
import boto3
from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key

client = boto3.client("dynamodb")
client.update_table(                      # add a GSI to an existing table
    TableName="Orders",
    AttributeDefinitions=[{"AttributeName": "status", "AttributeType": "S"},
                          {"AttributeName": "order_id", "AttributeType": "S"}],
    GlobalSecondaryIndexUpdates=[{"Create": {
        "IndexName": "status-index",
        "KeySchema": [{"AttributeName": "status", "KeyType": "HASH"},
                      {"AttributeName": "order_id", "KeyType": "RANGE"}],
        "Projection": {"ProjectionType": "INCLUDE", "NonKeyAttributes": ["total"]},
    }}],
)
# ...once the index is ACTIVE:
table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("Orders")
pending = table.query(IndexName="status-index",
                      KeyConditionExpression=Key("status").eq("PENDING"))
print([i["order_id"] for i in pending["Items"]])
takeaways: GSIs: any key, added any time, eventually consistent, own capacity
LSIs: same partition key, other sort key, created with the table, 10 GB per collection
Projections control which attributes an index returns
Items without the index key are simply absent from the index
pitfalls: Reading from a GSI immediately after a write and expecting to see the new item.

quiz.q: Which statement about global secondary indexes is true?
options: They are updated asynchronously, so index reads are eventually consistent
They can only be created along with the table
They support strongly consistent reads
Their keys must be unique
quiz.explain: GSIs are propagated asynchronously, so a just-written item may not appear in the index yet.

concepts.name: Batch reads and writes
concepts.summary: Read up to 100 items and write up to 25 per request with BatchGetItem and BatchWriteItem, and retry unprocessed items.
concepts.why: Batching cuts the number of trips to DynamoDB for bulk loads and reads of many items, but it has rules that silently lose data if ignored.
concepts.body:
Instead of one call per item, a **batch** sends many at once. `BatchWriteItem` sends up to **25** put or delete requests (no updates) across one or more tables in one call; `BatchGetItem` fetches up to **100** items by full primary key. Both are capped at 16 MB per call.

A batch is **not a transaction** (an all-or-nothing group of changes): each item succeeds or fails on its own, and there are no conditions. When DynamoDB is busy or slowing you down, it returns the leftovers as **unprocessed items**, in `UnprocessedItems` (writes) or `UnprocessedKeys` (reads). You must send those again, ideally waiting a little longer after each try. Code that ignores them loses writes without any exception.

In Python, the **batch writer** (`table.batch_writer()`) handles this for you: it collects puts and deletes in a **buffer** (a holding list in memory), sends them in groups of 25 and resends unprocessed items automatically. `overwrite_by_pkeys=[...]` removes repeated keys from the buffer (a batch may not contain the same key twice).

Batches save network **round trips** (a request out and a reply back), not capacity: each item still costs the same read or write units as an individual call. `BatchGetItem` reads are eventually consistent unless you set `ConsistentRead` per table, and results come back in no particular order.

To load a lot of data into a new table, **Import from S3** (CSV, DynamoDB JSON or Ion files) is faster and uses no write capacity.
concepts.code:
import boto3

ddb = boto3.resource("dynamodb")
table = ddb.Table("Orders")

with table.batch_writer() as batch:          # chunks of 25, retries leftovers
    for n in range(60):
        batch.put_item(Item={"customer_id": "c7", "order_id": f"o{n:03}", "n": n})

keys = [{"customer_id": "c7", "order_id": f"o{n:03}"} for n in (1, 2, 3)]
resp = ddb.batch_get_item(RequestItems={"Orders": {"Keys": keys}})
print(sorted(int(i["n"]) for i in resp["Responses"]["Orders"]))   # [1, 2, 3]
print(resp["UnprocessedKeys"])   # {}  -> otherwise resend these
takeaways: BatchWriteItem: up to 25 puts/deletes; BatchGetItem: up to 100 gets
Batches aren't all-or-nothing; resend UnprocessedItems/UnprocessedKeys
`batch_writer()` batches and resends for you
Batching saves round trips, not capacity units
pitfalls: Calling the low-level batch_write_item and never checking UnprocessedItems.

quiz.q: A BatchWriteItem call returns non-empty UnprocessedItems. What should the caller do?
options: Nothing; DynamoDB retries them later
Switch to Scan
Roll back the processed items
Resend those items, waiting a little longer after each try
quiz.explain: Unprocessed items were not written; the client must retry them itself.

concepts.name: Capacity modes and read consistency
concepts.summary: On-demand versus provisioned capacity, how reads and writes are counted, throttling, and eventually versus strongly consistent reads.
concepts.why: Capacity decides your bill and your throttling behaviour; consistency decides what a read can return.
concepts.body:
DynamoDB counts work in **capacity units**:

- one **read unit** = one strongly consistent read per second of an item up to **4 KB** (eventually consistent reads cost half)
- one **write unit** = one write per second of an item up to **1 KB**
- sizes round up per item: a 5 KB write costs 5 units, a 5 KB strong read costs 2
- transactional reads and writes (all-or-nothing groups, covered later) cost double

In **on-demand mode** you pay per request, and DynamoDB absorbs sudden spikes up to double the previous peak at once, growing beyond that more gradually; you can set a maximum to cap cost. It's the recommended default. With **provisioned capacity** you set the read and write units per second yourself (RCU and WCU), usually with auto scaling adjusting them; it's cheaper for steady, predictable traffic. You can switch between the two.

When requests exceed the capacity available, DynamoDB **throttles** them: it refuses them with `ProvisionedThroughputExceededException` or `ThrottlingException`. The SDKs retry automatically, waiting longer each time. Throttling that won't go away usually means one **hot key** (one partition key getting most of the traffic) rather than too little capacity overall.

**Consistency**: by default `GetItem`, `Query` and `Scan` are **eventually consistent** and may miss a write from the last moment. `ConsistentRead=True` gives a strongly consistent read that reflects every successful write, at twice the cost; it isn't available on GSIs (secondary indexes) or in Streams.
concepts.code:
# Capacity arithmetic (per item, rounded up):
#
#   item 3 KB  strong read          ceil(3/4) = 1 RCU
#   item 3 KB  eventual read        0.5 RCU
#   item 9 KB  strong read          ceil(9/4) = 3 RCU
#   item 2.5 KB write               ceil(2.5/1) = 3 WCU
#   item 2.5 KB transactional write 2 * 3 = 6 WCU
#
# Query reading 40 items of 1 KB (40 KB total, strong):  40/4 = 10 RCU
# (a Query sums item sizes first, then rounds up to 4 KB)

import boto3
table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("Orders")
r = table.get_item(Key={"customer_id": "c1", "order_id": "o1"},
                   ConsistentRead=True, ReturnConsumedCapacity="TOTAL")
print(r["ConsumedCapacity"])   # {'TableName': 'Orders', 'CapacityUnits': 1.0}
takeaways: Reads are metered in 4 KB, writes in 1 KB steps
Eventual reads cost half; transactions cost double
On-demand is the default choice; provisioned capacity suits steady traffic
Strong reads cost 2x and are unavailable on GSIs
pitfalls: Storing large, rarely read attributes in frequently written items, multiplying write cost by item size.

quiz.q: How many write units does writing one 2.5 KB item cost (non-transactional)?
quiz.explain: Write units are per 1 KB rounded up, so 2.5 KB costs 3 units.

concepts.name: Designing from access patterns
concepts.summary: Model a DynamoDB table by listing access patterns first, then shaping keys, often with several entity types in one table.
concepts.why: Relational habits produce slow, expensive DynamoDB tables; access-pattern-first design is what makes it scale.
concepts.body:
In a relational database you usually start from the things you store (customers, orders), give each its own table and avoid storing anything twice; questions come later and are answered with joins. DynamoDB design runs the other way:

- write down every **access pattern**, with its inputs: "get user by id", "list a user's orders newest first", "get an order with its line items", "list open orders for a warehouse"
- choose keys so each pattern is a single `GetItem` or `Query` on the table or an index
- **denormalize**: copy data into several items where that saves a read

A common technique is **single-table design**: store several kinds of items in one table with generic key names (`PK`, `SK`) and prefixed values. A customer and their orders share a partition key, so one query fetches a customer together with their orders, which is DynamoDB's substitute for a join:

- customer: `PK = CUST#42`, `SK = PROFILE`
- order: `PK = CUST#42`, `SK = ORDER#2025-03-01#A17`
- line item: `PK = ORDER#A17`, `SK = ITEM#1`

Querying `PK = CUST#42` returns the profile and all orders; adding `begins_with(SK, "ORDER#")` returns only the orders.

Single-table design is a tool, not a rule. Separate tables are fine when items are never fetched together, and they're easier to understand, back up and stream. The goal is that every frequent request is one call against a well-spread key.
concepts.code:
import boto3
from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("App")   # keys: PK (S), SK (S)
with table.batch_writer() as b:
    b.put_item(Item={"PK": "CUST#42", "SK": "PROFILE", "name": "Ann"})
    b.put_item(Item={"PK": "CUST#42", "SK": "ORDER#2025-01-09#A11", "total": 20})
    b.put_item(Item={"PK": "CUST#42", "SK": "ORDER#2025-03-01#A17", "total": 35})

# access pattern: customer with all orders, one request
both = table.query(KeyConditionExpression=Key("PK").eq("CUST#42"))["Items"]
print([i["SK"] for i in both])
# ['ORDER#2025-01-09#A11', 'ORDER#2025-03-01#A17', 'PROFILE']

# access pattern: latest order only
last = table.query(KeyConditionExpression=Key("PK").eq("CUST#42")
                   & Key("SK").begins_with("ORDER#"), ScanIndexForward=False, Limit=1)
print(last["Items"][0]["total"])   # 35
takeaways: List access patterns before choosing keys
Every frequent request should be one GetItem or Query
Pre-join related items by giving them the same partition key
Prefixed generic keys (PK/SK) let one table hold many kinds of items
pitfalls: Normalizing into many tables and then doing several sequential reads, or scans, to assemble one screen.

quiz.q: In single-table design, how do you fetch a customer together with their orders in one request?
options: Use a JOIN in PartiQL
Give the profile and orders the same partition key and Query it
Scan with a filter on customer id
Create a transaction across two tables
quiz.explain: Items sharing a partition key form one item collection, which a single Query returns.

concepts.name: Transactions
concepts.summary: Group up to 100 actions across items and tables into an all-or-nothing TransactWriteItems or a consistent TransactGetItems.
concepts.why: Some rules span several items, such as moving a balance between accounts or keeping emails unique, and need writes that succeed or fail together.
concepts.body:
A **transaction** is a group of changes that succeed or fail together. `TransactWriteItems` runs up to **100** actions (Put, Update, Delete, ConditionCheck) on different items, in one or more tables of the same account and Region, **atomically**: either all succeed or none apply. Each action can have its own condition; if any condition fails, the whole transaction is cancelled with `TransactionCanceledException`, whose `CancellationReasons` tell you which action failed. `ConditionCheck` checks something about an item you don't change.

`TransactGetItems` reads up to 100 items as one consistent snapshot.

Things to know:

- the total size limit is 4 MB, and one item can't appear twice in a transaction
- transactional operations cost **twice** the normal capacity
- a transaction can be cancelled when another write touches the same items at the same time; retry it
- pass a `ClientRequestToken` so that retrying the same transaction within 10 minutes can't apply it twice: the retry is **idempotent**

A classic use is keeping a non-key attribute unique: write the user item and a second marker item with `PK = EMAIL#ann@x.com`, both guarded by `attribute_not_exists`, in one transaction.

Transactions are powerful but expensive; many designs need only single-item conditional writes.
concepts.code:
import boto3

client = boto3.client("dynamodb")

def register(user_id, email):
    client.transact_write_items(TransactItems=[
        {"Put": {"TableName": "App",
                 "Item": {"PK": {"S": f"USER#{user_id}"}, "SK": {"S": "PROFILE"},
                          "email": {"S": email}},
                 "ConditionExpression": "attribute_not_exists(PK)"}},
        {"Put": {"TableName": "App",          # uniqueness marker for the email
                 "Item": {"PK": {"S": f"EMAIL#{email}"}, "SK": {"S": "EMAIL"}},
                 "ConditionExpression": "attribute_not_exists(PK)"}},
    ])

register("u1", "ann@example.com")
try:
    register("u2", "ann@example.com")    # email taken: nothing is written
except client.exceptions.TransactionCanceledException as e:
    print([r["Code"] for r in e.response["CancellationReasons"]])
    # ['None', 'ConditionalCheckFailed']
takeaways: Up to 100 actions, all-or-nothing, across tables in one region
Any failed condition cancels the whole transaction
Transactions cost double and can conflict; retry with a ClientRequestToken
Marker items plus transactions enforce uniqueness of non-key attributes
pitfalls: Using transactions for every write by default, doubling cost where a single conditional write was enough.

quiz.q: A TransactWriteItems with three Puts fails the condition on the second Put. What is written?
options: Nothing
The first and third Puts
The first Put only
All three, with a warning
quiz.explain: Transactions are atomic: one failed condition cancels every action.

concepts.name: Sparse indexes, overloading and sharding
concepts.summary: Advanced key patterns: sparse indexes, overloaded GSI keys, inverted indexes, and write sharding to spread very busy keys.
concepts.why: These patterns let a few indexes serve many access patterns and keep heavy traffic evenly spread.
concepts.body:
A few patterns come up in nearly every serious DynamoDB design:

- **Sparse index**: only items that have the index's key attribute are indexed. Set `open_since` only on open orders, and a GSI on it lists exactly the open ones; remove the attribute when the order closes and it drops out. Small, cheap, and a natural to-do list of work.
- **GSI overloading**: give the index generic keys (`GSI1PK`, `GSI1SK`) and let each kind of item put its own meaning in them: orders by `STATUS#PENDING`, users by `EMAIL#...`. One index then answers many questions, which matters because each GSI adds write cost.
- **Inverted index**: a GSI whose partition key is the table's sort key and the other way round, so many-to-many links can be read from both sides (the students on a course, the courses of a student).
- **Write sharding**: if one key value gets too much traffic (a global leaderboard, today's date), add a suffix to it, random or calculated, such as `DATE#2025-03-01#7`, to spread it over N **shards** (separate key values). When reading, query all N shards and combine the results.

Also consider **composite sort keys** like `COUNTRY#STATE#CITY`, so `begins_with` queries at any level work from one index.

Every pattern costs something: duplicated storage, extra writes, more complex reads. Add them for real access patterns only.
concepts.code:
import random
import boto3
from boto3.dynamodb.conditions import Key

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("App")   # GSI "GSI1" on (GSI1PK, GSI1SK)
SHARDS = 4

def record_vote(day, user):
    shard = random.randrange(SHARDS)               # spread one hot day over 4 keys
    table.put_item(Item={"PK": f"VOTE#{user}", "SK": day,
                         "GSI1PK": f"DAY#{day}#{shard}", "GSI1SK": user})

def votes_for(day):
    items = []
    for s in range(SHARDS):                        # read every shard
        items += table.query(IndexName="GSI1",
            KeyConditionExpression=Key("GSI1PK").eq(f"DAY#{day}#{s}"))["Items"]
    return items

for u in ["ann", "bob", "cy"]:
    record_vote("2025-03-01", u)
print(sorted(i["GSI1SK"] for i in votes_for("2025-03-01")))   # ['ann', 'bob', 'cy']
takeaways: Sparse GSIs index only items that carry the key attribute
Overloaded GSI keys (generic names) let one index serve many patterns
Inverted indexes read many-to-many relations from both sides
Write sharding spreads a busy key; reads must query every shard
pitfalls: Sharding a key that is not actually hot, which only multiplies read requests.

quiz.q: Why is a GSI on an attribute that only open orders have called a sparse index?
options: It stores only every tenth item
It only exists in one Availability Zone
It uses compressed storage
Items lacking the attribute are not copied into the index
quiz.explain: Index entries exist only for items that have the index key, so the index holds just the open orders.

concepts.name: Streams and TTL
concepts.summary: React to every item change with DynamoDB Streams and Lambda, and expire items automatically with Time to Live.
concepts.why: Reacting to changes and cleaning up old data automatically are core building blocks of serverless DynamoDB apps.
concepts.body:
**DynamoDB Streams** is a log of every change to a table's items (insert, modify, remove), kept in order per item for **24 hours**. The `StreamViewType` decides what each record carries: `KEYS_ONLY`, `NEW_IMAGE`, `OLD_IMAGE` or `NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES` (the item after the change, before it, or both).

The usual reader is **AWS Lambda**, through an event source mapping: Lambda checks the stream for new records and calls your function with groups of them. Use it to keep running totals up to date, keep a search index in sync, send notifications, or copy changes to another store.

Records for the same item arrive in order. If your function raises an error, Lambda calls it again with the same group of records, so handlers must be **idempotent**: handling a record twice must do no harm. Configure a failure destination and `BisectBatchOnFunctionError` (which splits a failing group to find the bad record) so one bad record can't hold up everything behind it. For longer retention and more readers, send the changes to Kinesis Data Streams instead.

**Time to Live (TTL)**: pick an attribute that holds an expiry time as a **Unix timestamp**, the number of seconds since 1 January 1970. After that moment DynamoDB deletes the item in the background, free of charge, usually within a few days rather than instantly. When it matters, skip expired-but-not-yet-deleted items in your queries (`expires_at > :now`). TTL deletions show up in the stream with a `userIdentity` of `dynamodb.amazonaws.com`, so you can archive expired items to S3.
takeaways: Streams keep 24 hours of ordered item changes; Lambda is the usual reader
Stream handlers are retried, so make them idempotent
TTL takes seconds since 1970 as a number and deletes expired items for free
TTL deletion is delayed; filter out expired items if exactness matters
pitfalls: Storing the TTL attribute as a date string or in milliseconds; TTL then never deletes the item.

quiz.q: An item's TTL attribute passed an hour ago. What can a query still return?
options: Never the item; deletion is exact to the second
An error until the item is deleted
Possibly the item, because TTL deletes in the background with a delay
Only the key attributes
quiz.explain: TTL deletion is asynchronous and can lag, so expired items may still be read until removed.

concepts.name: Partitions, hot keys and adaptive capacity
concepts.summary: How DynamoDB stores data in partitions, the per-partition throughput limits, and how adaptive capacity and splits handle heat.
concepts.why: Hot partitions are the main cause of throttling at scale, and fixing them requires knowing how data is physically placed.
concepts.body:
Internally a table is split into **partitions**, each stored on SSDs and replicated across three AZs. The partition key's hash places each item. A partition holds up to about **10 GB** and serves up to **3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second**. These limits apply per partition regardless of how much capacity the table has overall.

So a table can have plenty of total throughput and still throttle if traffic concentrates on one key, a **hot key**. DynamoDB mitigates this in several ways:

- **adaptive capacity** instantly lends unused throughput to busy partitions, up to the per-partition maximums
- **split for heat**: a partition that stays hot is split, spreading its key range across more partitions (this cannot spread a single partition key value that is itself too hot, unless the sort key range can be divided)
- partitions are added as data grows or provisioned capacity increases, and are never merged back

What this means for design: a single partition key value has a ceiling of about 1,000 writes/s, so very hot values need write sharding or a **cache** (a fast copy of popular results kept in front of the table). CloudWatch Contributor Insights shows the most accessed and throttled keys. Throttled requests in metrics such as `ThrottledRequests` with low overall consumption point to a key-distribution problem, not a capacity problem.

LSIs pin an item collection to one partition, hence their 10 GB limit.
takeaways: Each partition: about 10 GB, 3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU per second
One hot partition key can throttle while the table has spare capacity
Adaptive capacity and split for heat help, but cannot fix one ultra-hot key
Use Contributor Insights to find hot keys; shard or cache them
pitfalls: Raising table capacity to cure throttling caused by a single hot key.

quiz.q: An on-demand table throttles writes while total consumption is low. Most likely cause?
options: The table is too small
Writes concentrate on one partition key beyond per-partition limits
On-demand tables cannot exceed 1,000 writes/s in total
TTL is enabled
quiz.explain: Per-partition limits apply to each key's partition, so a hot key throttles regardless of table totals.

concepts.name: Global tables and multi-Region
concepts.summary: Replicate a table across AWS Regions, understand conflict resolution and consistency choices, and plan failover.
concepts.why: Global tables give low-latency local access worldwide and Region-level resilience, but change your consistency model.
concepts.body:
A **global table** is a set of replica tables in several AWS Regions that DynamoDB keeps in sync. Every replica accepts reads and writes (**multi-active**), so users in each Region get local latency and an application can fail over by sending traffic to another Region.

With the default **multi-Region eventual consistency** (MREC), a write is acknowledged in its own Region and replicated to the others asynchronously, typically within a second. If the same item is written in two Regions concurrently, conflicts are resolved by **last writer wins**: the write with the later timestamp is kept everywhere and the other silently disappears. Designs therefore often send each item's writes to a single "home" Region, or use writes that give the same result in any order (like adding to a counter).

Global tables can alternatively be configured for **multi-Region strong consistency** (MRSC), across three Regions, where a write is synchronously replicated and strongly consistent reads in any Region see the latest value, at the cost of higher write latency and some feature restrictions. Check the current docs for supported Regions and limitations.

Other points:

- conditional writes and transactions evaluate in the local Region only (transactions are not atomic across Regions under MREC)
- replicated writes consume write capacity in every Region
- TTL and streams work per replica; a TTL deletion replicates like any delete

Plan failover with Route 53 (AWS's DNS service) or your app's own logic for choosing a Region, and test it.
takeaways: Replicas in several Regions, all read/write
MREC: async replication, last writer wins on conflicts
MRSC: synchronous, strongly consistent across Regions with higher latency
Transactions and conditions are Region-local; writes are paid in every Region
pitfalls: Allowing the same item to be updated from several Regions under MREC and losing updates to last-writer-wins.

quiz.q: Under eventual-consistency global tables, two Regions update the same item at the same time. What happens?
options: The write with the later timestamp wins everywhere
Both updates are merged attribute by attribute
Both Regions roll back
The table enters a read-only state
quiz.explain: Conflicts are resolved by last writer wins, so one concurrent update is discarded.

concepts.name: Item size, caching and cost control
concepts.summary: Work within the 400 KB item limit, offload large blobs to S3, cache with DAX, and keep read and write costs predictable.
concepts.why: At scale the bill is driven by item size and request patterns, and design choices can change it by an order of magnitude.
concepts.body:
Item size multiplies cost: every write is billed per 1 KB and every read per 4 KB. Patterns that keep items lean:

- put large blobs (documents, images) in **S3** and store only the object key
- **vertical partitioning**: split a big entity into several items under one partition key (`SK = PROFILE`, `SK = SETTINGS`, `SK = HISTORY#...`) so frequent updates touch small items
- compress large text attributes (gzip into a binary attribute) when you must keep them inline
- keep attribute names short in huge tables; names count toward item size

The hard limit is **400 KB** per item, including attribute names.

**DAX** (DynamoDB Accelerator) is a **cache** in front of DynamoDB: a cluster of machines that keeps recently read items in memory and speaks the same API, giving microsecond reads for read-heavy, repetitive access. It's write-through: writes pass through it to the table, so it stays current. It serves only eventually consistent reads and is one more cluster to run; for many apps a cache inside the application, or simply reading less, is enough.

Other levers: use eventually consistent reads where possible (half price), project only needed attributes into GSIs, delete unused GSIs, use the **Standard-IA** table class for rarely accessed data (cheaper storage, pricier requests), switch steady workloads to provisioned capacity with auto scaling or reserved capacity (a discount for committing in advance), and watch `ConsumedReadCapacityUnits` per operation using `ReturnConsumedCapacity`.
concepts.code:
import gzip
import boto3

table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table("App")
doc = ("lorem ipsum " * 4000).encode()          # ~48 KB of text

table.put_item(Item={"PK": "DOC#1", "SK": "BODY",
                     "body_gz": gzip.compress(doc)})   # binary attribute
r = table.put_item(Item={"PK": "DOC#1", "SK": "META", "title": "Notes", "views": 0},
                   ReturnConsumedCapacity="TOTAL")
print(r["ConsumedCapacity"]["CapacityUnits"])   # 1.0  small item, cheap updates

body = gzip.decompress(table.get_item(
    Key={"PK": "DOC#1", "SK": "BODY"})["Item"]["body_gz"].value)
print(len(body) // 1000, "KB raw,", len(gzip.compress(doc)), "bytes stored")
# 48 KB raw, 142 bytes stored  (repetitive text compresses well)
takeaways: Item size drives cost: writes per 1 KB, reads per 4 KB; max item 400 KB
Store blobs in S3 and split big entities into several items
DAX caches eventually consistent reads in microseconds
Eventual reads, lean GSI projections and table classes cut cost
pitfalls: Incrementing a view counter inside a 300 KB item, paying 300 write units per click.

quiz.q: A 200 KB item has a counter updated 100 times per second. What is the cheapest fix?
options: Use strongly consistent reads
Switch to Scan
Add a GSI on the counter
Move the counter into its own small item under the same partition key
quiz.explain: Each update is billed on the full item size, so a separate 1 KB item cuts write cost about 200 times.
